extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, cultural economics, and social theory; general readers of Veblen's The Theory of the Leisure Class
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and standards from a sociological/theoretical chapter on consumption, taste, devout observance, and leisure (Veblen). Focus is on how pecuniary canons and conspicuous waste shape habits, taste, and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propensity for emulation (invidious comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propensity for emulation--for invidious comparison--is of ancient growth and is a pervading trait of human nature, and (with the exception of self-preservation) is probably the strongest and most alert and persistent of the economic motives proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This propensity is readily called into vigorous activity in any new form and, once habitual expression exists, is extremely tenacious; it directs individuals toward honorific expenditure and resists relinquishing established conspicuous expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous consumption / conspicuous waste as regulatory norm
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulating norm of consumption is in large part the requirement of conspicuous waste: visible, honorific expenditure acts to absorb increases in industrial efficiency or output after material wants are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In communities where conspicuous consumption is part of the scheme of life, an individual's increased ability to pay will tend to take the form of expenditure on accredited lines of conspicuous consumption; this channels economic activity toward ostentatious displays rather than material comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted standard of expenditure determines standard of living
rubrics_metrics.description: The accepted standard of expenditure in the community or class largely determines an individual's standard of living by commending itself as right and good and by exerting social pressure (propriety, fear of ostracism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards are internalized through habitual contemplation of the scheme of life; conformity is both agreeable and expedient, often indispensable for comfort and success in life—resulting in expenditure being 'as high as the earning capacity of the class will permit' and with a constant tendency to rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of accredited canons of consumption (prescriptive usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the selective surveillance of the law of conspicuous waste there grows up a code of accredited canons of consumption that holds the consumer to a standard of expensiveness and wastefulness in goods and in the employment of time and effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These canons operate both on public consumption and on many private, ostensibly serviceable articles (e.g., underclothing, kitchen utensils) where added cost and commercial value do not proportionately increase serviceability; they shape habits of thought about what is honest, reputable, beautiful, and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks of expensiveness are conflated with beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The marks of expensiveness come to be accepted as beautiful features of an object; our pleasure in these marks (signifying honorific costliness) blends with appreciation of intrinsic beauty so that we often attribute beauty to what is largely an indication of expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This blending complicates discrimination between serviceability and wastefulness; fashion and reputability codes determine what forms and materials are 'beautiful' at a given time, and an inexpensive but intrinsically beautiful object may be judged not beautiful because it lacks expensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility vs. honorific value tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects are often valued more for their honorific (conspicuous) utility than for their intrinsic serviceability; costly objects may be less effective for ostensible purposes yet are preferred because they signal status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a hand-wrought silver spoon may be less serviceable than a cheaper machine-made spoon but is prized for its costliness and status; spurious imitations greatly reduce the honorific utility and thus the perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous consumption shapes morals and attitudes toward property
rubrics_metrics.description: The canon of honorific expenditure influences the code of morals—especially the sacredness of property—so that wealth's meritoriousness and conspicuous spending can mitigate moral opprobrium for offenses against property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We are prone to condone offenses that secure a 'decent' manner of life for dependents; the well-spent booty of a successful wrongdoer can gain social approbation, and large wealth may soften legal or moral penalties in popular judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicarious consumption and vicarious leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuous consumption frequently operates vicariously: one person's consumption (or leisure) is performed on behalf of another (the owner/master) to enhance the master's pecuniary repute; priestly vestments and servitors exemplify vicarious consumption and vicarious leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vicarious consumption leads to accessories and rituals that emphasize ostentation without serving the consumer's comfort; vicarious leisure (servitors performing unproductive, perfunctory service) signals the master's elevated status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devout consumption shaped by pecuniary canons (austerity as honorific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious/devout consumption conforms to pecuniary canons: sanctuaries, vestments, and ritual often favor conspicuous waste; the fittings of worship are expected to be above reproach and may be intentionally austere or discomforting as an honorific sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devout austerity and costly but comfortless paraphernalia serve as vicarious consumption—designed not to enhance worshippers' comfort but to enhance the pecuniary repute of the divine or the cult; ritual perfunctoriness also signals vicariousness and unprofitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfunctoriness of ritual and priestly demeanor as status markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Priestly demeanor—aloof, leisurely, perfunctory, uncontaminated by sensuous pleasure—is itself a mark of vicarious leisure and honorific status; ritual reduces to rehearsed, pro forma service which pleases devout taste as evidence of exaltation above profane industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of agile or dexterous execution in priestly office is valued because it implies the master (divinity) is above productive service; similar analogies apply to household servants whose unproductivity signals the master's standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-specific codes of pecuniary beauty and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Different social classes hold different codes of reputability that define what is appropriate as honorific consumption; tastes (in flowers, dress, furniture, houses, gardens) vary by class not due to intrinsic aesthetic endowment but due to differing pecuniary codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is admired as beautiful in one class may be deemed vulgar in another; the code determines which objects lie within the scope of honorific consumption for that class and thus shapes aesthetic evaluations and fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and selective conspicuousness in domestic life
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the emphasis on visible consumption, domestic life tends to be relatively shabby compared to the éclat of public displays, and people habitually screen private consumption from observation; where private consumption can be hidden, individuals often withdraw from neighborly contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selective surveillance produces exclusiveness and reserve in domestic life and contributes to demographic effects (e.g., lower birthrates among classes required to maintain reputable expenditure for children).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absorption of productivity gains into conspicuous expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: As industrial efficiency increases, the saved labor and incremental wealth are channeled not into less toil but into greater conspicuous expenditure; individuals direct efforts to larger acquisition of wealth to meet endlessly expansible honorific wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where this does not happen, it is often because wealth increases too rapidly for expenditure habits to adjust, or because conspicuous consumption is deferred to heighten spectacle; the general tendency is that output increments feed conspicuous waste rather than comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptitudes and inherited propensities shape habitual consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmitted aptitudes and specific facilities of expression influence how rapidly individuals form habits (e.g., alcoholism, devout observances, romantic love), and aptitudes that align with honorific expenditure result in tenacious habits important to well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When material means increase, individuals' longstanding propensities and existing forms of expression (aided by current accredited schemes of life) will shape the direction of new expenditures toward familiar honorific lines.
